tur54-0: What is lumbar spinal stenosis, how is it recognised, why do the legs hurt when walking, and does narrowing on MRI need surgery? A review of the evidence, a short history, the place of physiotherapy, six home exercises and warning signs.
tur54-1: The diagnosis is mostly made from your history and an examination. According to a review published in JAMA in 2022, no single finding is both highly sensitive and highly specific on its own; the findings are assessed together.
tur54-3: Buttock and leg pain that increases when standing and walking and eases when sitting or bending forward is typical; being able to walk more comfortably when leaning on a shopping trolley is often described. Having no low back pain while sitting and problems with balance are also among the findings that support the diagnosis.
tur54-4: Walking with the feet set wide apart (wide-based gait) or loss of balance with the eyes closed (a positive Romberg test) strongly supports the diagnosis (specificity over 90%); however, these findings are seen in only about 40% of patients. Loss of sensation, strength or reflexes is found in about half of patients.
tur54-5: Usually not needed for the initial diagnosis and initial treatment; it is requested to confirm the diagnosis and clarify the anatomy when an injection or surgery is being considered. If there are urgent warning signs, MRI or CT is done straight away. An X-ray shows slipping of a vertebra or curvature of the spine; MRI is preferred for detailed assessment. Narrowing on imaging does not on its own determine the treatment decision.
tur54-6: From recognition as a separate condition to today
tur54-7: Lumbar spinal stenosis was described as a separate condition in the 1950s. Studies in recent years have supported exercise and physiotherapy as the first treatment; they have shown that the benefit of cortisone injections is short-lived and that the superiority of surgery over non-surgical treatment is not clear.
tur54-8: Verbiest described narrowing of the lumbar canal as a separate condition: patients' pain appeared with movement and disappeared when sitting or lying down.
tur54-9: Verbiest published his findings in English (JBJS, "A radicular syndrome from developmental narrowing of the lumbar vertebral canal").
tur54-10: In a study of 400 patients (NEJM), adding cortisone to a local anaesthetic injection gave little or no benefit at week 6.
tur54-11: In a study of 169 surgical candidates (Ann Intern Med), there was no significant difference in physical function between surgery and physiotherapy after 2 years; 57% of the physiotherapy group had surgery during this time.
tur54-12: A Cochrane review of five studies (643 patients) reported that no firm conclusion can be drawn on whether surgery is better than non-surgical treatment.
tur54-13: In a study of 259 patients with an average age of 72 (JAMA Netw Open), individualised exercise together with manual therapy improved symptoms and walking capacity at 2 months more than medical care or group exercise; at 6 months there was no difference between the groups.
tur54-14: A review published in JAMA: an estimated 103 million people worldwide live with symptomatic spinal stenosis; first treatment is activity modification, pain control and physiotherapy.
tur54-15: Getting pain under control may make it easier to keep exercising and walking. Ask your physician which painkillers are suitable for you.
tur54-16: The assessment of a review published in JAMA in 2022. Treatment is chosen according to the person, the severity of symptoms and how much daily life is limited.
tur54-19: How posture affects symptoms is explained; activities that keep the back bent forward, such as cycling or side-stroke swimming, may be suggested.
tur54-20: First-line treatment. In one study, supervised physiotherapy led to improvement in more people than home exercise at week 6 (63% vs 33%); exercise together with manual therapy was found helpful in some studies, and at 6 months there was no difference between the groups.
tur54-21: There are few definitive studies specific to spinal stenosis. Ask your physician which is suitable for you.
tur54-22: It may give limited relief lasting a few weeks; benefit lasting 6 weeks or longer appears unlikely. Although rare, there is a risk of serious infection and permanent nerve damage.
tur54-23: Decompression is considered for people whose pain and functional limitation persist despite non-surgical treatment. In one study the benefit at 2 years was modest: 7.8 points more improvement on the Oswestry disability scale (0–100) than with non-surgical treatment, against a clinical importance threshold of 11–12.8 points. Whether to add bone fusion when a vertebra has slipped is debated: in one study, decompression alone was not inferior to decompression with fusion (at least 30% improvement in disability score: 71.4% vs 72.9%).
tur54-24: Usually not needed for the initial diagnosis and initial treatment; the diagnosis is mostly made from your history and an examination. According to a review published in JAMA in 2022, imaging is requested to confirm the diagnosis and clarify the anatomy when an injection or surgery is being considered. If there are urgent warning signs, MRI or CT is done straight away. An X-ray shows conditions that may affect treatment, such as slipping of a vertebra or curvature of the spine; MRI is preferred for detailed assessment. Because narrowing on imaging is also seen in many people without symptoms, the treatment decision is not based on the image alone.
tur54-25: Seek help without delay in the following situations; how urgent each is, is shown at the start of each group.
tur54-26: Go to the emergency department or call 112 immediately:
tur54-27: Being unable to pass urine, or loss of bladder or bowel control
tur54-28: Numbness or loss of sensation around the buttocks, groin or genitals
tur54-29: New leg weakness or numbness together with a fever or a history of cancer
tur54-30: Back pain after a traffic accident or a fall from a height
tur54-31: Sudden, severe leg pain together with coldness, paleness or a change of colour
tur54-32: Back pain together with a fever
tur54-33: Severe back pain after a simple fall in someone with osteoporosis
tur54-34: Back pain together with unexplained weight loss or a history of cancer
tur54-35: Weakness or numbness in the legs that is slowly getting worse
tur54-36: Leg pain that does not ease even at rest
